endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Some AI solutions warrant periodic retraining or competency assessment—particularly when the AI model is updated, when clinical evidence about the tool's performance changes, or when the clinical context of use shifts.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether refresher training or competency reassessment after a material AI update or a shift in context of use changes clinician behavior or patient outcomes. The recommendation currently rests on one governance framework (CHAI) that uses "should" language, and no supplied study documents how often the targeted hazard occurs.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so a GRADE certainty rating cannot be assigned. The single endorsement is expert guidance, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect. Any claim that retraining reduces errors after model updates remains untested in the supplied material.

The targeted failure is a clinician who applies an outdated mental model to an updated tool. No supplied study measures how often this happens, how severe the resulting harm is, or whether retraining catches it before it reaches patients. Without that information, the size of the safety benefit is unknown.

The CHAI playbook names three triggers for retraining or competency assessment: model updates, changes in clinical evidence about performance, and shifts in context of use. It frames the practice as warranted for some AI solutions rather than all of them, which leaves each health system to decide which updates count as material.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare clinician accuracy, reliance, and override behavior before and after material AI updates, with and without refresher training. They should also define thresholds for a material update or context shift and measure the frequency of errors caused by outdated understanding.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether context-of-use shifts toward these populations would be recognized as triggers for retraining, or whether training would address performance differences in these groups.
